pages.title: Primer on Latency & Bandwidth: Speed of Light
bulletPoints: Latency: The time it takes for a packet to travel from source to destination (governed strictly by the speed of light).
Bandwidth: The maximum data throughput of the communication path (governed by network capacity and frequency modulation).
Speed of light in fiber optics: Light travels at ~200,000 km/s in glass (approx. 33% slower than in a vacuum).
The core bottleneck: Bandwidth has grown exponentially over the decades, but latency remains bound by physics.
pages.footerText: Page 1 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: TCP Fundamentals: Three-Way Handshake & RTT
bulletPoints: Three-Way Handshake: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK establishes a stateful, reliable, bi-directional byte stream.
Latency cost: The initial handshake imposes a full Round-Trip Time (RTT) penalty before any data bytes can be transmitted.
TCP Fast Open (TFO): Enables data exchange inside the initial SYN packet using cryptographic cookies to save 1 RTT.
Keep-Alive: Reusing existing connections is the single most important network optimization for web performance.
pages.footerText: Page 2 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: TCP Congestion Control: Slow Start & AIMD
bulletPoints: Congestion Window (cwnd): Limits the total number of unacknowledged packets that the sender may transmit.
Slow Start: cwnd starts small (initially 10 packets) and doubles every RTT (exponential growth: 10 -> 20 -> 40 -> 80).
Congestion Avoidance: Once packet loss occurs or ssthresh is reached, cwnd transitions to Additive Increase / Multiplicative Decrease (AIMD).
Impact on web: Short, bursty HTTP requests often terminate while still trapped in Slow Start without reaching full bandwidth.
pages.footerText: Page 3 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: TCP Tuning: Window Scaling, SACK & Tail Loss Probe
bulletPoints: Window Scaling (RFC 1323): Extends the 16-bit receive window up to 1GB to saturate high-bandwidth, high-latency links.
Selective Acknowledgment (SACK): Allows receiver to acknowledge non-contiguous packet blocks, eliminating full retransmissions.
Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN): Routers mark packet headers to signal congestion before packet drops happen.
Tail Loss Probe (TLP): Quickly retransmits lost tail packets to prevent long retransmission timeouts (RTO).
pages.footerText: Page 4 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: UDP Fundamentals: Stateless Datagram Transport
bulletPoints: User Datagram Protocol (UDP): Lightweight, connectionless transport offering zero connection overhead.
No guarantees: UDP provides no retransmission, no in-order delivery, no flow control, and no congestion control.
Application control: Audio/video streaming, multiplayer gaming, and DNS prefer UDP to avoid TCP head-of-line blocking.
Foundation for QUIC: The modern web builds custom reliability, security, and flow control on top of raw UDP datagrams.
pages.footerText: Page 5 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: TLS/SSL Primer: Public Keys, Certificates & Trust
bulletPoints: Transport Layer Security (TLS) provides confidentiality (encryption), integrity (tamper detection), and authentication.
Asymmetric cryptography (RSA / Elliptic Curve): Used during handshake to securely exchange symmetric session keys.
Symmetric cryptography (AES-GCM / ChaCha20-Poly1305): Used for high-speed hardware-accelerated bulk payload encryption.
Certificate Authorities (CAs): Sign public keys to prove server identity against cryptographically verified trust roots.
pages.footerText: Page 6 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: TLS Handshake Evolution: 2-RTT to 1-RTT & 0-RTT
bulletPoints: Legacy TLS 1.2: Required 2 full round trips for cipher negotiation and key exchange before the first encrypted byte.
Modern TLS 1.3: Redesigned handshake completes in exactly 1 RTT by sending key shares in the initial ClientHello.
Zero Round-Trip Time (0-RTT): Returning clients resume connections and transmit early encrypted data in 0 RTT.
Replay attacks in 0-RTT: Early data is vulnerable to replay attacks; only idempotent requests (GET) should use 0-RTT.
pages.formulaOrSummary: TLS 1.2 = 2 RTTs | TLS 1.3 = 1 RTT | TLS 1.3 Resumption = 0 RTT
pages.footerText: Page 7 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: Optimizing TLS: Session Resumption & ALPN
bulletPoints: Session Tickets (RFC 5077): Encrypted state tickets sent to the client to avoid server-side session caching across clusters.
Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN): Negotiates the protocol (HTTP/2, HTTP/3) inside the TLS handshake.
OCSP Stapling: Server caches signed certificate revocation proofs from the CA to eliminate client OCSP lookups.
Forward Secrecy: Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) ensures compromised long-term private keys cannot decrypt past sessions.
pages.footerText: Page 8 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: Wireless & Mobile Networks: Cellular Radios & RRC
bulletPoints: Radio Resource Control (RRC): State machine managing phone battery power and cellular network radio connectivity.
RRC States: Idle (low power, radio disconnected), Cell_FACH (medium power), and Cell_DCH (high power, dedicated channel).
Tail timer penalty: Radios stay in high-power Cell_DCH for 10-15 seconds after network traffic stops, draining battery.
Packet bursting: Group network requests together into rapid bursts to allow the mobile radio to return to low-power Idle.
pages.footerText: Page 9 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: Optimizing for Mobile: Intermittent Networks & Battery
bulletPoints: Eliminate periodic polling: Polling every 60 seconds keeps the cellular radio continuously in high-power state, killing battery.
Adopt server push: Use WebSockets, Server-Sent Events, or push notifications to deliver messages only when events occur.
Prefetch strategically: Download content anticipated during the active session while the radio is already awake.
Resilient retry logic: Expect sudden network drops when users walk into elevators or switch between Wi-Fi and 5G.
pages.footerText: Page 10 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: HTTP/1.1 Evolution: Keep-Alive & Domain Sharding
bulletPoints: HTTP/1.0 created a new TCP connection for every file; HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent Keep-Alive connections.
Head-of-Line (HoL) Blocking at HTTP layer: Only one request/response transaction can be active on a TCP connection at a time.
Workaround hacks: Domain sharding (splitting assets across 4 subdomains), CSS image sprites, and JS asset bundling.
Pipelining failure: HTTP pipelining attempted to queue requests, but buggy proxies caused responses to misalign.
pages.footerText: Page 11 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: HTTP/2 Architecture: Binary Framing & Multiplexing
bulletPoints: Binary Framing Layer: Replaces plain text with binary frames (HEADERS, DATA, SETTINGS, PING, RST_STREAM).
Streams and multiplexing: Multiple independent bi-directional streams interleave across a single shared TCP connection.
Elimination of HTTP HoL blocking: Heavy image downloads no longer block lightweight API JSON responses.
Stream lifecycle: Streams are numbered (odd for client-initiated, even for server-initiated) and can be reset without closing TCP.
pages.footerText: Page 12 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: HTTP/2 Stream Prioritization & Dependency Trees
bulletPoints: Clients can declare stream dependencies and assign integer weights (1 to 256) to prioritize critical resources.
Critical assets first: HTML and critical CSS receive high priority; background images and analytics scripts receive low priority.
Dependency tree: If resource A depends on resource B, the server allocates bandwidth to B before transmitting A.
Server implementation challenges: Misconfigured proxies often ignore prioritization trees, causing suboptimal delivery.
pages.footerText: Page 13 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: HTTP/2 Header Compression: HPACK Algorithm
bulletPoints: HTTP headers are repetitive (Cookies, User-Agent, Accept headers repeat on every single asset request).
HPACK compression: Employs a Static Table (common HTTP headers) and a Dynamic Table (discovered during the session).
Huffman coding: Employs static Huffman tables to compress string characters into fewer bits.
Bandwidth savings: Reduces header overhead by over 85%, significantly accelerating mobile web browsing.
pages.footerText: Page 14 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: HTTP/2 Server Push: Mechanics & Limitations
bulletPoints: Server Push allows a server to send resources to the client cache before the client even parses the HTML and requests them.
PUSH_PROMISE frame: Informs the client of intent to push an asset; client can send RST_STREAM if already cached.
Real-world issues: Pushing assets already present in browser cache wastes bandwidth; 103 Early Hints has largely superseded push.
Cache-digest proposals: Attempted to solve over-pushing by transmitting a bloom filter of cached assets.
pages.footerText: Page 15 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: The Limits of TCP: Transport-Layer Head-of-Line Blocking
bulletPoints: HTTP/2 solved HTTP-layer HoL blocking, but could not fix TCP-layer Head-of-Line blocking.
TCP guarantee: TCP guarantees strictly in-order delivery of the underlying byte stream.
The single packet drop problem: If 1 TCP packet is dropped, the OS kernel buffers all subsequent streams until retransmission.
Worse on lossy networks: On a lossy 2% cellular network, multiplexed HTTP/2 can perform slower than multiple HTTP/1.1 connections.
pages.footerText: Page 16 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: HTTP/3 & QUIC: Re-Inventing Transport on UDP
bulletPoints: QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections): Designed from scratch by Google and standardized by IETF as the foundation of HTTP/3.
Runs entirely on UDP: Bypasses OS kernel TCP stack constraints, allowing rapid user-space innovation and deployment.
Independent stream transport: Packet loss on Stream A does NOT pause or delay packet processing on Stream B.
Native encryption: TLS 1.3 is baked directly into the QUIC transport packet header rather than running as a layered protocol.
pages.formulaOrSummary: HTTP/3 = HTTP Semantics + QUIC (Independent Streams + Embedded TLS 1.3) + UDP
pages.footerText: Page 17 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: QUIC Innovations: Connection Migration & Faster Recovery
bulletPoints: Connection ID (CID): Connections are identified by a 64-bit CID rather than the traditional 4-tuple (IP, port).
Seamless connection migration: When moving from home Wi-Fi to 5G cellular, active downloads continue without breaking.
Improved packet numbering: Every packet has a monotonically increasing packet number, eliminating retransmission ambiguity.
Monotonic acknowledgments: Precise RTT measurements prevent spurious retransmissions.
pages.footerText: Page 18 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: Browser Networking Internals: Sockets & Speculation
bulletPoints: Speculative preconnect: Modern browsers predict user navigation based on hover/typing and open TCP+TLS connections early.
DNS prefetching: `<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="//cdn.example.com">` resolves domain IP addresses in the background.
Resource preloading: `<link rel="preload" as="font" href="...">` fetches critical web fonts before CSS renders.
103 Early Hints: Server sends preliminary 103 HTTP status while generating HTML, allowing browser to preload subresources.
pages.footerText: Page 19 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: Resource Timing & Navigation Timing APIs
bulletPoints: PerformanceNavigationTiming: Measures high-resolution timestamps for redirect, DNS, TCP, TLS, TTFB, and DOM complete.
Time to First Byte (TTFB): Time from sending request to receiving the first byte of response; reflects server and network latency.
First Contentful Paint (FCP) & Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): Core Web Vitals measuring visual loading perception.
ResourceTiming API: Detailed network waterfall metrics for every individual script, style, image, and font resource.
pages.footerText: Page 20 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: WebSockets: Full-Duplex Bi-Directional Streaming
bulletPoints: HTTP Upgrade: Client starts with standard HTTP request with `Upgrade: websocket` and `Connection: Upgrade` headers.
Persistent framing: Establishes a lightweight, bi-directional framing channel over a single TCP socket.
Minimal overhead: Frame headers add only 2 to 10 bytes of overhead compared to hundreds of bytes in HTTP requests.
Best uses: High-frequency collaborative apps, real-time gaming, financial tickers, and live chat applications.
pages.footerText: Page 21 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: WebRTC Primer: Real-Time Audio, Video & P2P Data
bulletPoints: WebRTC (Web Real-Time Communication): Native browser API for peer-to-peer audio, video, and arbitrary binary data.
MediaStream: Captures camera and microphone input, handles hardware echo cancellation, noise suppression, and gain control.
RTCDataChannel: Peer-to-peer data channel supporting both reliable (TCP-like) and unreliable (UDP-like) delivery semantics.
Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP / SRTP): Encrypted media delivery optimized for sub-500ms interactive human conversations.
pages.footerText: Page 22 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: WebRTC Signaling & NAT Traversal (ICE, STUN, TURN)
bulletPoints: Signaling channel: WebRTC does not specify how peers find each other; developers exchange SDP offers/answers via WebSocket.
STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT): Discovers public IP addresses and port mappings behind consumer NAT routers.
TURN (Traversal Using Relays around NAT): Cloud relay server used as fallback when symmetric NATs block direct P2P connections.
Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE): Tests all candidate connection pairs to find the fastest direct path.
pages.formulaOrSummary: Direct P2P (STUN) -> Fallback to Cloud Relay (TURN)
pages.footerText: Page 23 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: WebRTC DataChannels: Reliable vs Unreliable Transport
bulletPoints: Built on SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) encapsulated inside DTLS over UDP.
Unreliable delivery option: Configure `maxRetransmits: 0` for game player positions; stale packets are discarded immediately.
Ordered vs unordered delivery: Disabling ordering requirement eliminates head-of-line blocking for independent updates.
Sub-100ms P2P gaming: Enables direct peer-to-peer gaming lobbies and decentralized file sharing.
pages.footerText: Page 24 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking

pages.title: The Performance Delivery Checklist: Modern Best Practices
bulletPoints: Deploy HTTP/3 & QUIC: Fallback gracefully to HTTP/2; enable TLS 1.3 with session resumption across all CDN edges.
Leverage CDNs: Move content closer to users to minimize physical round-trip speed-of-light propagation delays.
Optimize critical path: Inline critical CSS, preload hero images and key fonts, and defer non-essential JavaScript.
Embrace modern compression: Serve Brotli (br) for text assets and AVIF / WebP for visual media to minimize byte transfer.
pages.footerText: Page 25 of 25 · High Performance Browser Networking
